principle: Songs are temporary evidence. Albums, artists, scenes, and phases are the durable review layer.

worlds.title: PANICO NO SUBMUNDO
worlds.reason: Claude's DJ K pick makes sense as an album-sized test of what the Yeezus phase was really about: abrasion, distortion, menace, hard edits, or simply Kanye at that moment.
worlds.boundary: Choose Phase only if this is exciting as a bridge but not a world you want to keep exploring.
worlds.sourceReason: Smith identifies a scene-specific São Paulo bruxaria record—horror, metallic minimalism, and hard edits—not a generic ‘sounds like Yeezus’ match.

next.title: Radio Libertadora!
next.reason: Same producer, changed intent: more crowd-tested and overtly political. The review is a countercheck, not hype—it warns that this one is less cohesive and lyrically uglier.

worlds.title: Space 1.8
worlds.reason: This tests whether your electronic attention and quieter jazz listening belong to one durable taste: spacious, tactile, slowly changing music.
worlds.boundary: Calm or focus usefulness is not automatically Core.
worlds.sourceReason: Sherburne hears one coherent language joining jazz balladry, beat music, ambient drift, harp, and modular synth—the exact border this card is testing.

next.title: Endlessness
next.reason: The same composer’s second album tests whether you want her evolving musical world, not only the atmosphere of one acclaimed debut.

worlds.title: City of God (Original Soundtrack)
worlds.reason: Movies often organize your listening into scenes. This tests a complete Brazilian film world rather than extracting one soundtrack song.
worlds.boundary: A favorite film can still have a soundtrack you do not want outside the movie.
worlds.sourceReason: This starts from one of your confirmed film anchors. The supporting review describes heavy funk, space rock, and scene-setting music—not a generic Brazilian playlist.

next.title: Black Orpheus (Original Soundtrack)
next.reason: Another complete Brazil × cinema world tests whether film is a lasting portal into Brazilian music for you, not just a City of God association.

worlds.title: Now
worlds.reason: A whole-album test for the melodic, cinematic, global-psych side of your curiosity—not another isolated novelty track.
worlds.boundary: Want more can mean the scene interests you even if this exact record is not Core.
worlds.sourceReason: The trail begins with the record’s composer-producer, Korean rock pioneer Shin Jung-hyeon, so the recommendation can continue through a maker rather than an algorithmic mood.

next.title: Shin Jung-hyeon & Yup Juns, Vol. 1
next.reason: Follow the composer-producer behind Now into his own band. This asks whether Shin’s musical language—not only Kim Jung Mi’s voice—is what stays.

worlds.title: Abu Ali
worlds.reason: Long-form groove, live-feeling arrangement, and a complete cultural scene connect Fairuz-adjacent attention with jazz and Brazilian rhythmic listening.
worlds.boundary: Do not decide from the first minute; the long form is part of the question.
worlds.sourceReason: Ziad is Fairuz’s son and collaborator, and he built a Lebanese language from Arabic melody, jazz, funk, and classical music. That is a real family-and-creator trail.

next.title: Wahdon
next.reason: Return to Fairuz through Ziad’s writing and arrangements. It tests whether the connection works in song form as well as Abu Ali’s long instrumental groove.

worlds.title: Good Time (Original Motion Picture Soundtrack)
worlds.reason: This tests whether your newer electronic pull becomes stronger when it carries a film's pressure, pace, and damaged emotional atmosphere.
worlds.boundary: Separate loving a scene-making function from wanting the artist's wider catalog.
worlds.sourceReason: Geffen describes a score that builds the Safdies’ anxiety measure by measure. That directly tests your movie-shaped listening rather than abstract OPN similarity.

next.title: Uncut Gems (Original Soundtrack)
next.reason: Same composer-director partnership, a different pressure system. It tests whether this is a durable creative collaboration you follow across films.

worlds.title: The Sailor
worlds.reason: Your 88rising years contain many durable song returns. The album asks whether that was a lasting artistic world, an identity era, or both.
worlds.boundary: Nostalgia can be Core, but call it Phase only if you no longer want new work from this lane.
worlds.sourceReason: Reese hears Brian stretching into melodic, bittersweet, boom-bap, emo-rap, Spanish-guitar, and psych-rock modes. That makes this an album-growth test, not 88rising nostalgia bait.

next.title: Nicole
next.reason: Stay inside the 88rising generation but change artist and autobiography. This tests whether the durable part is the scene’s Asian-diaspora self-writing, not Rich Brian alone.

worlds.title: To Pimp a Butterfly
worlds.reason: This is the cleanest test of whether you love Kendrick primarily as songs, as a writer, or as an album-world builder.
worlds.boundary: A respected masterpiece is not automatically personal Core; answer for your actual desire to return.
worlds.sourceReason: The source is the people who made the record explaining its jazz, funk, writing, and construction—not a score telling you that a masterpiece must be your favorite.

next.title: Blackstar
next.reason: Producer Tony Visconti said Bowie’s team listened heavily to To Pimp a Butterfly while making Blackstar. This follows documented influence across genres, not sonic guesswork.
